prize_parts.citation: For developing the political-economy theory of trade policy, showing how organised interests shape the structure of trade protection.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B003 to B001. The reason is consistency in the standard I apply, not the number of colleagues who prefer B001. In round 1 I defended Obstfeld and Rogoff by separating the durable framework from the empirical fate of one specification, such as the Redux sticky-price assumptions. The main objection to B001 is the same kind: mixed and specification-sensitive support for the protection-for-sale predictions. Applying my own test, the contribution is that lobbying and tariff formation became a tractable, falsifiable equilibrium object, which produced three decades of theory, structural and reduced-form testing, and work on trade agreements. That meets the standard of originating a framework that reorganised a field. Attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: a long joint programme with joint papers and a book, two names, and no obvious omitted co-originator at the same level. By comparison, B003 has a less clean split between framework and puzzles, and B030 has the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum gap. Maturity is not in question. I would confine the citation to the political economy of trade protection, as the ballot's stated discovery does. That avoids borrowing from the innovation-and-growth strand, which may overlap with the 2025 prize, and avoids resting the award on a specification's empirical fit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. Structural estimates of protection-for-sale are sensitive to specification, so a narrow citation risks rewarding a research agenda more than a settled result. Trade was recognised in 2008, and a narrow citation on political economy is a more modest contribution than the full Grossman-Helpman programme. My own previous reading was that B003 stands on at least as good a footing on originality, and I have not shown it is weaker. Whether the intertemporal framework is distinct from Mundell-Fleming remains a judgement call, and I still regard that case as strong. Helpman's credit on both B001 and B030 requires an explicit choice about which trade line a prize would reward. Finally, my switch rests on general knowledge and colleagues' written descriptions, and I have not independently verified the empirical literature or the overlap with earlier prizes.

responses.point: Krusell finds the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale more worrying than the B001 supporters do. He thinks the lasting value may be as an organising theory, whereas BLP has been validated by three decades of practical use. He also warns against widening the B001 citation to endogenous growth.
responses.response: I now weigh the empirical record as he does and still reach a different conclusion. A framework that survives as an organising theory is the kind of contribution I defended for Obstfeld and Rogoff, so I cannot apply a harsher test to Grossman and Helpman without being inconsistent. I agree the citation should not extend to growth. I also accept that B002 is validated by use in a way B001 is not. But B002's three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan and Reiss, and as a macroeconomist I have no basis to adjudicate the identification debates in industrial organisation. I keep B002 out of my alternatives for that reason, not because I rate it lower on importance.

responses.point: Dreber prefers B030 because the firm-heterogeneity framework has been confronted with micro data more densely than protection-for-sale. She names the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as its main weakness, and treats Helpman's overlap as a choice between contributions, not a reason to split credit.
responses.response: I agree with her last point and have kept B030 as an alternative on that basis. The denser empirical record is a real advantage, and I ranked it second in my opening. I move it below B001 for attribution. I cannot see how a three-name citation resolves the exporter-facts gap without weakening the Melitz-Helpman core, and she says the same. I also read the testing record differently. The firm-heterogeneity facts were established before the theory, so part of the empirical confrontation measures how well the framework fits known facts, not how it predicted new ones. That is a difference of weighting, not a rejection of the case, and I would support B030 if the committee finds the attribution gap manageable.

responses.point: Fredriksson would build the B001 citation only on lobbying and trade protection. He says the endogenous-growth strand would invite overlap with 2025 and stretch the discovery beyond what the ballot defines. He also keeps B001 and B030 separate because of Helpman's overlap.
responses.response: I adopt his framing. In round 1 I objected to resting a prize on a strand the Academy has just recognised, and a citation limited to the political economy of protection removes that objection. It also addresses my worry about the Helpman overlap. B001 and B030 reward different contributions, so choosing B001 means choosing a different discovery, not a refinement of B030. I would add a caution to his wording: the citation should say the contribution is the framework and the empirical programme it created, not that predictions have been confirmed. His own reading of the mixed evidence points the same way.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B001 first. He anchors the citation on the political economy of trade policy and treats Helpman's separate firm-heterogeneity credit as a different achievement that a Grossman-Helpman award does not preclude.
responses.response: In round 1 I said the choice between the two trade lines must be made explicitly. I accept his answer: an explicit choice is possible without settling B030 first, because the two ballots credit different work. I disagree with part of his case. His list of colleagues who reached the same view independently does not count as merit, and I did not use it. What moved me are his points about clean attribution and about maturity. I also note that he is a close IIES colleague and a co-author of mine. I weigh his written arguments as I would any member's, and on the point where we differ I read the overlap with the 2025 prize as narrower than he does only if the citation stays confined to protection.

uncertainties: How much the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale should count against the award, once it is accepted that a framework is not the same as a specification. The committee's answer would decide whether B003 or B030 becomes preferable.

Whether a citation confined to the political economy of trade protection is distinct enough from Krugman's 2008 prize and from the 2025 innovation-and-growth prize. My information on both prizes comes from the files and general knowledge.
Whether Obstfeld and Rogoff would be judged a distinct discovery from Mundell-Fleming. I still see B003 as a close alternative on this question.
Whether Helpman's credit on both B001 and B030 should be treated as two independent achievements or as competing framings of one trade prize.
I have not independently verified citation, replication or impact data, and my judgement of B001's empirical record relies on general knowledge and colleagues' written assessments.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred configuration (Helpman, Grossman) from the supplied profile. For disclosure, my profile lists long-running co-authorship with Peter Klenow (credited on B037, not in my configuration), with Philippe Aghion, and a collaboration with Fabrizio Zilibotti. None is credited on B001, B003 or B030. My collaboration with Aghion is relevant to how I judge overlap with the 2025 prize on innovation-led growth. It is a reason to keep the B001 citation confined to political economy, and I disclose it without adjudicating it. I am also an associate professor at IIES and a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and John Hassler, with no tie to any B001 credited name.
